entry: Genus of large theropod dinosaurs of the Late [[Cretaceous]] period, best known from *Tyrannosaurus rex*. The bipedal carnivore had a massive skull balanced by a long, heavy tail, and its two-clawed forelimbs were short but unusually powerful for their size. The most complete specimen measures 12.3–12.4 m (40–41 ft) long, although most modern estimates suggest it could have exceeded 13 m (43 ft). Its estimated bite force is the largest of any terrestrial animal. Fossils from the late Maastrichtian age, 69.4 to 66 million years ago, have been found across western North America, and it was among the last non-avian dinosaurs before the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event]]. Whether it was a predator or a scavenger was long debated, but most paleontologists now accept that it was a predator. Soft tissue and proteins have been reported in at least one specimen.

Family of [[Passerine|passerine]] birds native to the [[Americas]]. With more than 400 species, it is the world's largest bird family and the most diverse bird family in every country of the Americas except the United States and Canada. Members vary greatly in shape, size and color, though most species are plain brown, gray or white. The smallest, the short-tailed pygmy tyrant and black-capped pygmy tyrant of the genus *Myiornis*, measure 6.5–7 cm (2.6–2.8 in) and weigh 4 to 5 g. The largest is the great shrike-tyrant, at 29 cm (11 in). Most species are almost entirely insectivorous, and many North American species catch insects in mid-air by flying from a perch and returning to it. The name echoes that of the Old World flycatchers, to which the family is not closely related. It belongs to the suboscines, which lack the vocal capabilities of [[Songbird|songbirds]].

City in southern [[Lebanon]], capital of the Tyre District. One of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, Tyre was an early [[Phoenicia|Phoenician]] metropolis and the legendary birthplace of Europa. It is the fifth-largest city in Lebanon, after [[Beirut]], Tripoli, Sidon and Baalbek. The urban area had approximately 200,000 inhabitants in 2016, including refugees, as the city hosts three of the twelve Palestinian refugee camps in Lebanon. The original city stood on an island 500 to 700 metres offshore until [[Alexander the Great]] built a causeway in 332 BCE, which the modern city now covers. Ancient sites include a hippodrome, and the city was added to the [[UNESCO]] World Heritage list in 1984. The name possibly means "rock" in Semitic languages.

Reddish-purple [[Dye|dye]] secreted by predatory sea snails of the family Muricidae. The name refers to the ancient [[Phoenicia|Phoenician]] city of Tyre. Extracting it required tens of thousands of snails, making the dye costly and a marker of status. Production began by the Phoenicians as early as 1200 BC and continued under the Greeks and Romans until the [[Fall of Constantinople|fall of Constantinople]] in 1453. The color did not easily fade and grew brighter with weathering and sunlight. Sumptuary laws restricted purple garments, and senior Roman magistrates wore togas edged in it.

American actor known for swashbuckling and romantic roles. Born in [[Cincinnati]], Ohio, he appeared in dozens of films, including *Jesse James*, *The Mark of Zorro*, *Blood and Sand* and *Nightmare Alley*. He was best known on stage for *John Brown's Body* and *Mister Roberts*. He served in the [[United States Marine Corps]] during [[World War II]], rising to captain and fighting at the [[Battle of Iwo Jima]]. He died of a heart attack in [[Madrid]], [[Spain]], while filming *Solomon and Sheba*. He was posthumously honored with a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]].

Genus of [[Owl|owls]], including the barn owls, in the family Tytonidae. It is the most widely distributed owl genus, found almost everywhere except polar and desert regions and Asia north of the [[Himalayas]]. Most species measure 33–39 cm (13–15 in) in length, with large, heart-shaped facial discs and mottled gray or brown upperparts. Barn owls hunt mainly small mammals by sound, mostly at night. Pairs often mate for life, and the female incubates an average clutch of four eggs laid in a hollow tree, an old building or a cliff. Populations can expand rapidly when prey is plentiful. Authorities disagree on how many species the genus contains; the International Ornithological Committee recognizes four. The barn owl is listed as Least Concern globally, though some subspecies with restricted ranges are more threatened.

Irish rock band formed in Dublin in 1976, with lead vocalist [[Bono]] and guitarist the Edge. Its anthemic music and politically conscious lyrics made it renowned globally for live performances by the mid-1980s, highlighted by its appearance at [[Live Aid]] in 1985. *The Joshua Tree* (1987) was its greatest success, selling 25 million copies. The band reinvented its sound in the 1990s with *Achtung Baby* (1991), influenced by alternative and electronic dance music. It has released 15 studio albums, sold an estimated 170 million records and won 22 [[Grammy Awards]].

Governing body of [[Association football|association football]] in Europe, one of [[FIFA]]'s six continental confederations. Its 55 member associations, 48 of them sovereign UN member states, run national and club competitions such as the [[UEFA Champions League]], the European Championship and the Nations League. UEFA was inaugurated on 15 June 1954 in [[Basel]], Switzerland, and has been headquartered in Nyon since 1995. Its members include transcontinental countries such as [[Turkey]] and [[Russia]].

Annual club [[Association football|association football]] competition organized by [[UEFA]] for top-division European clubs. It is the most-watched club competition in the world and the third most-watched football competition overall, after the [[FIFA World Cup]] and the [[UEFA European Championship]]. Introduced in 1955 as the European Champion Clubs' Cup, it took its current name in 1992 and added a group stage in 1991. The present format has 36 teams in a single league phase, with the top 24 advancing to knockout rounds that end in a final. Spanish clubs have the most victories, with 20, followed by England with 15. Real Madrid is the most successful club, having won it 15 times.

Primary [[Association football|association football]] tournament organized by [[UEFA]], informally called the Euro. Contested by the senior men's national teams of member associations, it is the second-most watched football tournament after the [[FIFA World Cup]]. Originally called the European Nations' Cup, it took its current name in 1968. Spain has won four titles, the most of any team, and Germany has won three. Spain is the only team to win consecutive titles, in 2008 and 2012. From the 2020 edition, the winner plays the [[Copa América]] champion in the Finalissima.

Specification for the firmware architecture of a computing platform. The firmware typically runs first when a computer is powered on, before the [[Operating system|operating system]] or any other program loads. UEFI replaced the BIOS on [[IBM]] PC-compatible computers, though it can provide backward compatibility through CSM booting. Unlike the BIOS, which IBM originally developed as proprietary, UEFI is managed by an industry consortium. Intel developed the original Extensible Firmware Interface (EFI) and contributed it to the Unified EFI Forum in 2005. Version 2.3.1 added Secure Boot. The reference implementation, TianoCore EDK II, is written in [[C (programming language)|C]].

Specialized agency of the [[United Nations]] for education, science and culture. Headquartered in [[Paris]], it has 194 member states and 11 associate members. It was founded in 1945 as the successor to the International Committee on Intellectual Cooperation of the [[League of Nations]]. Its work is organized into five programme areas: education, natural sciences, social and human sciences, culture, and communication and information. UNESCO sponsors projects that improve [[Literacy|literacy]], protect press freedom and preserve regional and cultural history. It administers the World Heritage Convention and helps establish and secure [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage Sites]]. Its General Conference meets biannually to set programs and budget, and it appoints a Director-General every four years. Critics have argued that its decisions are politically biased; the United States withdrew in 1984 and 2017 and rejoined in 2023.

[[United Nations]] agency providing humanitarian and developmental aid to [[Child|children]] worldwide. Originally the United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund, it was created in 1946 to provide relief to children and mothers affected by [[World War II]]. Its mandate was extended in 1950 to address the long-term needs of children and women, particularly in developing countries. In 1953 it became a permanent part of the United Nations system and was renamed the United Nations Children's Fund, though it kept the acronym. UNICEF operates in 192 countries and territories, providing immunizations, [[HIV]] treatment, nutrition, [[Sanitation|sanitation]], education and emergency relief. It relies entirely on voluntary contributions from governments and private donors, and it was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1965.

Address of a resource on the [[World Wide Web]], also called a web address, specifying where it is located and how to retrieve it. A URL is a type of Uniform Resource Identifier (URI), though the terms are often used interchangeably. It is most commonly used for web pages ([[HTTP]] and [[HTTPS]]) but also for file transfer, email and database access. In https://www.example.com/index.html, https is the protocol, www.example.com the hostname and index.html the file name. Defined in RFC 1738 in 1994 by [[Tim Berners-Lee]] and the IETF's URI working group, it combines the domain name system with file path syntax.

Industry standard for digital data transmission and power delivery between computers, peripherals and hubs. Developed by the USB Implementers Forum and introduced in 1996, USB replaced serial and parallel ports on personal computers and has since replaced most common connectors. It has four generations of specifications: USB 1.x, USB 2.0, USB 3.x and USB4. Signaling rates range from 1.5 and 12 Mbit/s in USB 1.0 and 1.1 to 80 Gbit/s in USB4 2.0. USB Power Delivery supplies up to 240 watts and has become the standard charging format for many mobile phones. The [[USB-C]] connector can replace all earlier USB connectors.

24-pin reversible connector that supersedes all earlier [[USB]] connectors. Unlike those connectors, which had distinct host and peripheral ends, a USB-C cable connects either way. The design was developed in 2012 by members of the USB Implementers Forum with [[Intel]], HP Inc. and Texas Instruments, and the Type-C specification was published in 2014. The connector is not itself a protocol. It can carry data, video and power, as well as other protocols such as [[DisplayPort]], [[HDMI]] and Thunderbolt. A device's capabilities depend on the protocols it supports. The USB4 specification, released in 2019, can be used only through USB-C.

Battleship of the Pennsylvania class of the US Navy, sunk in the [[Attack on Pearl Harbor|attack on Pearl Harbor]] in 1941. Commissioned in 1916, she stayed in the United States during [[World War I]] but escorted President [[Woodrow Wilson]] to the Paris Peace Conference. She was based at Pearl Harbor from April 1940. On 7 December 1941, Japanese aircraft hit her with armor-piercing bombs. One detonated a magazine, sinking the ship and killing 1,177 officers and crewmen. Too badly damaged to be repaired for service in [[World War II]], her wreck lies beneath the USS Arizona Memorial, built across it.

Three-masted wooden [[Frigate|heavy frigate]] of the United States Navy, the oldest naval vessel still afloat. Launched in 1797 in [[Boston]], she was one of six frigates authorized by the Naval Act of 1794. Her first duties were protecting American merchant shipping and fighting Barbary pirates. She earned the nickname "Old Ironsides" after capturing HMS Guerriere in the [[War of 1812]], and she took several other British warships in that war. During the [[American Civil War]], she served as a training ship for the Naval Academy. Designated a museum ship in 1907, she has sailed under her own power on special anniversaries.

Battleship of the United States Navy that exploded and sank in [[Havana]] Harbor in 1898. Sent to protect U.S. interests during the Cuban War of Independence, she lost 268 sailors, about three-quarters of her crew. The sinking helped precipitate the [[Spanish–American War]], and the phrase "Remember the Maine!" became a rallying cry. A U.S. Navy board blamed an external mine, but others suggested a fire in a coal bunker. A 1974 investigation by Hyman Rickover supported the fire explanation, and the cause remains debated. The wreck was refloated in 1911 and sunk at sea. Its main mast is a memorial in Arlington National Cemetery.

Variable-width character encoding for [[Unicode]] that is backward compatible with [[ASCII]]. The name is short for Unicode Transformation Format – 8-bit. UTF-8 supports all 1,112,064 valid Unicode code points using one to four one-byte code units. ASCII characters use a single byte with the same value, so an ASCII file is also a valid UTF-8 file. Ken Thompson outlined the design in 1992 on a placemat in a New Jersey diner, with Rob Pike. It is used by nearly all webpages and is the dominant encoding on the [[World Wide Web]].

Former U.S. Highway running from [[Chicago]] to Santa Monica, California. Established on November 11, 1926, it was one of the original U.S. Highways and covered 2,448 miles (3,940 km) through eight states. It became a major route for westward migration, especially during the [[Dust Bowl]] of the 1930s. Traffic declined as the [[Interstate Highway System]] bypassed towns, and the highway was removed from the U.S. Highway System in 1985. Nicknamed the "Mother Road" by [[John Steinbeck]] in *The Grapes of Wrath* (1939), it is preserved in part as Historic Route 66, a National Scenic Byway. It also featured in the 2006 animated film *Cars*.

Constituent political entity of the United States, of which there are 50. Each state holds jurisdiction over a defined territory and shares sovereignty with the federal government, so Americans are citizens of both the federal republic and their state. States are divided into [[County (United States)|counties]] or county equivalents. States are represented in the [[United States Congress]] and select electors for the Electoral College. Congress admits new states, each on an equal footing with the others. The Supreme Court held in *Texas v. White* (1869) that the Constitution does not permit unilateral secession. The balance of state and federal power remains debated.

German submarine, especially one operated by the navy in [[World War I]] or [[World War II]]. The term anglicizes *Unterseeboot* ("undersea boat"). U-boats waged unrestricted submarine warfare against the [[United Kingdom]] to disrupt merchant traffic. In World War I a 1915 campaign was abandoned, and the 1917 resumption failed mainly because of convoys, though it contributed to the entry of the [[United States]] into the war. In World War II, [[Karl Dönitz]] focused on convoy battles in the [[Battle of the Atlantic]], but improved tactics turned the tide, and by May 1943 losses outpaced U-boat sinkings.

River of Central Africa, the largest right-bank tributary of the [[Congo River]]. It flows west, forming the border between the [[Central African Republic]] and the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]]. It passes Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic, then forms the boundary between the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the [[Republic of the Congo]] before joining the Congo at Liranga. The river is about 1,060 km (660 mi) long, or 2,270 km (1,410 mi) including the Uele, its longest tributary. Its drainage basin covers about 651,915 sq km (251,706 sq mi). It is an important transport artery between [[Bangui]] and [[Brazzaville]]. A 1960s plan, Transaqua, proposed diverting its water to revitalize [[Lake Chad]].

American ride-hailing and food delivery company headquartered in [[San Francisco]]. Garrett Camp conceived the idea in 2009 to make direct transportation easier and cheaper, and the service launched publicly in San Francisco in 2011. Originally called UberCab, the company changed its name after complaints from local [[Taxi|taxi]] operators. It is the largest ridesharing company in the world, with over 202 million monthly active users, and it operates in about 70 countries. Uber also provides [[Courier|courier]] services and [[Freight transport|freight transport]]. It has partnered with carmakers including [[Nissan]] and with [[Nvidia]] on robotaxi services.
